lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: Pressure, Archimedes' principle, upthrust and floatation
objectives: Define pressure and calculate it from normal force and area.
Explain hydrostatic pressure and calculate pressure at a depth in a liquid.
State Archimedes' principle and calculate upthrust from displaced fluid or apparent loss of weight.
Determine relative density using apparent-weight measurements.
Explain the laws of floatation and calculate the fraction of a floating body's volume that is submerged.
lessons.body:
PRESSURE
Pressure is the normal force acting per unit area:
P = F/A
where P is pressure in pascals (Pa), F is the perpendicular force in newtons (N), and A is area in square metres (m²). One pascal is one newton per square metre (1 Pa = 1 N/m²). For the same force, a smaller contact area produces greater pressure.

PRESSURE IN LIQUIDS
A liquid at rest exerts pressure on the walls and bottom of its container. At a depth h below the free surface:
P = ρgh
where ρ is the liquid density in kg/m³, g is gravitational field strength in m/s² and h is depth in metres. This is gauge pressure due to the liquid column; atmospheric pressure is additional if absolute pressure is required.

For a liquid at rest:
- Pressure increases with depth.
- At the same depth in the same connected liquid, pressure is equal.
- Pressure at a point acts in all directions.
- For a given depth, pressure increases with the density of the liquid.
- The hydrostatic pressure depends on density, depth and g, not on the shape of the container.

Worked example 1
A force of 40 N acts normally on an area of 5 m².
P = F/A = 40/5 = 8 Pa.

Worked example 2
Find the gauge pressure due to water at a depth of 0.5 m. Take ρ = 1,000 kg/m³ and g = 10 m/s².
P = ρgh = 1,000 × 10 × 0.5 = 5,000 Pa.

ARCHIMEDES' PRINCIPLE AND UPTHRUST
When a body is partly or completely immersed in a fluid, the fluid exerts an upward force on it called upthrust or buoyant force. Archimedes' principle states that the upthrust equals the weight of the fluid displaced by the body.

Upthrust = weight in air − apparent weight in the fluid.
For a fully immersed body:
Upthrust = ρfluid × g × Vdisplaced.
The displaced volume equals the volume of the immersed part of the body.

A body seems to weigh less when immersed because the upthrust acts upwards against its weight. The actual gravitational weight of the body has not changed; its apparent weight is reduced.

RELATIVE DENSITY USING ARCHIMEDES' PRINCIPLE
For a solid weighed in air and then fully immersed in water:
RD of solid = weight in air / (weight in air − apparent weight in water).
For a solid weighed in air, water and a test liquid:
RD of test liquid = (weight in air − apparent weight in test liquid) / (weight in air − apparent weight in water).
Use the same solid and ensure it is fully immersed without touching the container.

Worked example 3
A solid weighs 15 N in air and 10 N when fully immersed in water.
Upthrust = 15 − 10 = 5 N.
RD of solid = 15/5 = 3.

LAWS OF FLOATATION
A body floats in equilibrium when the upthrust equals its weight. By Archimedes' principle, this means:
weight of floating body = weight of fluid displaced.
A body with average density less than the fluid density can float with part of its volume above the surface. A body denser than the fluid sinks unless another force supports it.

For a uniform floating body:
fraction of volume submerged = density of body / density of fluid.
The fraction is dimensionless and must be between 0 and 1 for a body floating partly submerged.

Worked example 4
A wooden block has average density 600 kg/m³ and floats in water of density 1,000 kg/m³.
Fraction submerged = 600/1,000 = 0.6.
Therefore 60% of its volume is below the water surface.

Applications
- Ships float because their average density, including the air spaces in the hull, is less than the density of the water displaced.
- A hydrometer floats at different levels in liquids of different densities.
- Submarines control their average density by taking in or expelling water from ballast tanks.
- A life jacket increases a person's average volume without adding much mass, helping the person float.

Simple safe investigation
Measure a small object's weight using a spring balance in air, then lower it gently until it is fully immersed in water without touching the bottom or sides. Record the apparent weight. The difference is the upthrust. Use a light object, keep electrical equipment away from water, and wipe spills immediately.

practice.question: Define pressure, write its formula and state its SI unit.
practice.answer: Pressure is the normal force per unit area: P = F/A. Its SI unit is the pascal (Pa), equal to N/m².

marking.criterion: Defines pressure as normal force per unit area.

practice.question: A normal force of 40 N acts on an area of 10 m². Calculate the pressure.
Calculate the gauge pressure due to water at a depth of 0.2 m. Take water density as 1,000 kg/m³ and g = 10 m/s².

marking.criterion: Substitutes the values with correct units.

practice.question: A solid weighs 15 N in air and has an apparent weight of 10 N when fully immersed in water. Find the upthrust and the relative density of the solid.
practice.answer: Upthrust = 15 − 10 = 5 N. RD = weight in air/upthrust = 15/5 = 3.

marking.criterion: Uses RD = weight in air / loss of weight in water.

practice.question: State Archimedes' principle and write an expression for upthrust on a fully immersed body.
practice.answer: A body partly or wholly immersed in a fluid experiences an upthrust equal to the weight of fluid displaced. Upthrust = ρfluid g Vdisplaced.

marking.criterion: States that upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced.

practice.question: State the law of floatation and explain why a body floats partly submerged.
practice.answer: A floating body displaces a weight of fluid equal to its own weight. It floats partly submerged when its average density is less than the fluid density, so the required upthrust is reached before it is fully immersed.

marking.criterion: States weight of floating body equals weight of fluid displaced.
Relates floating to upthrust balancing weight.
Explains partial immersion using lower average density.

practice.question: A wooden block of average density 600 kg/m³ floats in water of density 1,000 kg/m³. What fraction of its volume is submerged?
practice.answer: Fraction submerged = density of block/density of water = 600/1,000 = 0.6 (60%).

lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: Work, energy and power
objectives: Define work done and calculate work for a force parallel or inclined to displacement.
Explain energy and distinguish kinetic and gravitational potential energy.
Apply KE = ½mv² and PE = mgh in calculations.
Explain conservation and transformation of energy.
Define power and calculate it from work or energy transferred per unit time.
lessons.body:
WORK DONE
Work is done when a force causes a displacement. For a constant force acting in the direction of displacement:
W = Fd
where W is work in joules (J), F is force in newtons (N) and d is displacement in metres (m). If a force acts at an angle θ to the displacement:
W = Fd cosθ.
Only the component of force along the displacement does work. If there is no displacement, the work done by that force is zero.

ENERGY
Energy is the capacity to do work. It is measured in joules (J). Energy can be transferred from one object or store to another and can change from one form to another. Common forms include mechanical, thermal, chemical, electrical, light, sound and nuclear energy.

MECHANICAL ENERGY
Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energy.
- Kinetic energy is energy due to motion:
  KE = ½mv²
- Gravitational potential energy is energy due to position/height in a gravitational field:
  PE = mgh
where m is mass in kilograms (kg), v is speed in metres per second (m/s), g is gravitational field strength in m/s² and h is height in metres (m).

LAW OF CONSERVATION OF ENERGY
Energy is not created or destroyed; it is transferred or transformed from one form to another. In an ideal system with no energy losses, total mechanical energy (KE + PE) remains constant. In real systems, some mechanical energy is often transferred to thermal energy and sound by friction or air resistance.

Worked example 1: work against gravity
A learner of mass 50 kg climbs stairs through a vertical height of 3 m. Take g = 10 m/s².
Work done against gravity = mgh = 50 × 10 × 3 = 1,500 J.

Worked example 2: kinetic energy
An object of mass 5 kg moves at 15 m/s.
KE = ½mv² = ½ × 5 × 15² = 562.5 J.

POWER
Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy:
P = W/t = E/t
where P is power in watts (W), W is work in joules (J), E is energy transferred in joules (J), and t is time in seconds (s).
For a constant force acting in the direction of motion at speed v:
P = Fv.

Worked example 3: power while climbing
A learner of mass 10 kg climbs a total vertical height of 2 m in 20 s. Take g = 10 m/s².
Work done = mgh = 10 × 10 × 2 = 200 J.
Power = work/time = 200/20 = 10 W.

ENERGY TRANSFORMATIONS
- A falling object: gravitational potential energy decreases while kinetic energy increases.
- A battery-powered lamp: chemical energy is transferred to electrical energy, then to light and thermal energy.
- A moving vehicle braking: kinetic energy is transferred mainly to thermal energy in the brakes and surroundings.
- A stretched spring released: elastic potential energy changes into kinetic energy.

UNIT AND CALCULATION CHECKS
- Work and energy: joule (J).
- Power: watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s.
- Force: newton (N); displacement: metre (m); time: second (s).
- Use the component of force parallel to displacement when the force is inclined.
- Keep mass in kilograms, speed in metres per second, height in metres and time in seconds when using SI formulae.

practice.question: Define work done in physics and state when work done by a force is zero.
practice.answer: Work is done when a force causes displacement. Work done by a force is zero if there is no displacement or if the force has no component along the displacement.

marking.criterion: Defines work as force causing displacement.
Mentions the force component in the direction of displacement.
States zero work when there is no displacement or no parallel force component.

practice.question: A learner of mass 50 kg climbs through a vertical height of 3 m. Calculate the work done against gravity. Take g = 10 m/s².
Calculate the kinetic energy of a 5 kg object moving at 15 m/s.
Find the gravitational potential energy gained by a 10 kg body raised vertically through 2 m. Take g = 10 m/s².
A 10 kg learner climbs a total vertical height of 2 m in 20 s. Calculate the average power developed against gravity. Take g = 10 m/s².
A 30 N force acts at 60° to the direction of a 5 m displacement. Calculate the work done by the force.

marking.criterion: Substitutes the force, displacement and angle correctly.

practice.question: A machine transfers 600 J of energy in 30 s. Calculate its average power.
Describe the main energy transformation as (a) a ball falls from a height and (b) a moving vehicle is brought to rest by its brakes.
practice.answer: (a) Gravitational potential energy decreases and kinetic energy increases. (b) Kinetic energy is transferred mainly to thermal energy in the brakes and surroundings, with some sound.

marking.criterion: Identifies potential-to-kinetic energy transfer for the falling ball.
Identifies kinetic-to-thermal (and sound) energy transfer during braking.

lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: Viscosity, fluid resistance and terminal velocity
objectives: Define viscosity as internal resistance to flow and distinguish it from density.
Explain fluid friction/drag and the coefficient/unit of dynamic viscosity at an introductory level.
Describe how fluid type and temperature affect viscosity.
Explain terminal velocity using the balance of weight, upthrust and viscous drag.
Identify practical applications of viscosity and plan a fair comparison investigation.
lessons.body:
VISCOSITY
Viscosity is the internal resistance of a fluid to flow. It describes how strongly adjacent layers of a liquid or gas resist sliding past one another. A fluid with high viscosity flows slowly under the same conditions; a fluid with low viscosity flows more easily. For example, honey is more viscous than water at the same room temperature.

VISCOSITY AND FLUID FRICTION
When a fluid flows, neighbouring layers exert frictional forces on one another. A body moving through a fluid also experiences drag, which acts opposite to its motion relative to the fluid. Viscosity is one important cause of this resistance.

The coefficient of dynamic viscosity, η (eta), measures a fluid's resistance to shearing flow. For a Newtonian fluid:
shear stress = η × velocity gradient.
The SI unit of dynamic viscosity is pascal-second (Pa·s), which is equivalent to N·s/m². At this level, use the coefficient as a measure of how readily a fluid flows; detailed calculations with the velocity gradient may be treated as an extension.

FACTORS AFFECTING VISCOSITY
- The nature of the fluid: different liquids and gases have different viscosities.
- Temperature: for most liquids, viscosity decreases as temperature increases, so warm oil flows more easily than cold oil. For gases, viscosity generally increases as temperature rises.
- Composition or concentration: dissolved or suspended materials can change a fluid's resistance to flow.

VISCOSITY AND TERMINAL VELOCITY
A body falling through a fluid experiences its weight downwards, upthrust upwards and viscous drag opposite to its motion. As the body speeds up, the drag usually increases. Eventually the upward drag and upthrust can balance the downward weight. The resultant force then becomes zero and the body continues at constant speed called terminal velocity.

At terminal velocity:
weight = upthrust + viscous drag.
The body is still moving, but its acceleration is zero because the forces balance.

APPLICATIONS OF VISCOSITY
- Engine oil is selected to lubricate moving parts while flowing through the engine.
- Thick lubricants remain between surfaces and reduce wear.
- Paint and printing ink are made to flow and spread at suitable rates.
- Food products such as honey and syrup are handled according to their flow properties.
- Shock absorbers use resistance to fluid flow to reduce unwanted bouncing.
- Knowledge of blood viscosity is important in understanding how blood flows through vessels.

Simple comparison investigation
Pour equal volumes of water and cooking oil through the same clean funnel, one at a time, at the same temperature. Measure the time each takes to flow into a measuring cylinder. Keep the funnel, volume and temperature the same. The fluid that takes longer to flow has the greater viscosity under those conditions. Repeat the test and average the times. Do not taste laboratory samples and wipe spills promptly.

VISCOSITY IS NOT DENSITY
Density is mass per unit volume. Viscosity is resistance to flow. A fluid may be dense without being highly viscous, or viscous without being especially dense. They are different physical properties and have different units.

practice.question: Define viscosity and state which is more viscous at room temperature: honey or water.
practice.answer: Viscosity is the internal resistance of a fluid to flow. Honey is more viscous than water at room temperature.

marking.criterion: Defines viscosity as internal resistance to flow.
Identifies honey as more viscous than water.

practice.question: Distinguish between density and viscosity.
practice.answer: Density is mass per unit volume, measured in kg/m³. Viscosity is a fluid's resistance to flow, with dynamic viscosity measured in Pa·s.

marking.criterion: Defines density as mass per unit volume.
Defines viscosity as resistance to flow.

practice.question: State two factors that affect viscosity and explain the effect of increasing temperature on most liquids.
practice.answer: Factors include the nature/composition of the fluid and temperature. For most liquids, viscosity decreases as temperature increases.

marking.criterion: States the nature/composition of the fluid as a factor.
Explains that most liquids become less viscous as temperature rises.

practice.question: Explain terminal velocity for a body falling through a fluid and state the force balance at that point.
practice.answer: As the body speeds up, viscous drag increases. At terminal velocity, acceleration is zero and weight is balanced by upthrust plus viscous drag: weight = upthrust + drag.

marking.criterion: Explains that drag increases as the body speeds up.
States that acceleration is zero and speed is constant.

practice.question: Give two practical applications where viscosity is important.
practice.answer: Examples include selecting engine lubricants, paint/ink flow, shock absorbers, food processing and blood flow.

marking.criterion: Gives a second distinct valid application.

practice.question: Describe a fair test for comparing the viscosity of water and cooking oil using a funnel and measuring cylinder.
practice.answer: Use equal volumes at the same temperature and the same clean funnel. Pour each fluid separately, measure the time taken to flow, repeat and average. The fluid taking longer to flow is more viscous under those conditions.

marking.criterion: Uses the same funnel and measures flow time.
Explains comparison/repeats and identifies longer time as higher viscosity.

practice.question: State the SI unit of dynamic viscosity and write the relation between shear stress and velocity gradient for a Newtonian fluid.
practice.answer: The SI unit is pascal-second (Pa·s). Shear stress = η × velocity gradient.

marking.criterion: Gives shear stress = η × velocity gradient.

lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: Thermometers, evaporation and boiling
objectives: Define a thermometer and thermometric property.
Describe five types of thermometer and the property each uses.
Compare mercury and alcohol and explain why water is unsuitable as a thermometric liquid.
Describe the clinical thermometer and safe handling.
Distinguish evaporation from boiling and state factors affecting evaporation.
Explain fixed points and solve simple thermometer-scale calculations.
Define absolute zero and state its value on Kelvin and Celsius scales.
lessons.body:
THERMOMETERS, EVAPORATION AND BOILING

1. Thermometer and thermometric property
A thermometer is an instrument for measuring temperature. A thermometric property is a measurable property that changes predictably with temperature, such as liquid-column length, gas pressure, electrical resistance or thermoelectric e.m.f.

2. Types of thermometer
- Liquid-in-glass thermometer: mercury or coloured alcohol; the length/volume of the liquid column changes with temperature.
- Constant-volume gas thermometer: a fixed mass of gas is kept at constant volume; its pressure changes with temperature.
- Thermoelectric (thermocouple) thermometer: two dissimilar metals produce a temperature-dependent e.m.f. at their junctions.
- Resistance thermometer: the electrical resistance of a metal wire changes with temperature.
- Bimetallic thermometer: two bonded metals expand by different amounts, bending the strip and moving a pointer.

3. Mercury and alcohol as thermometric liquids
Mercury advantages: it does not wet glass, is opaque and easy to see, expands fairly uniformly, conducts heat well and has a low freezing point (about −38.8 °C).
Mercury disadvantages: it is relatively expensive and cannot measure temperatures below its freezing point; mercury is also toxic and must be handled safely.
Alcohol advantages: it is inexpensive, expands more than mercury for a given temperature change and can measure much lower temperatures because its freezing point is very low.
Alcohol disadvantages: it wets glass, is colourless unless dyed, evaporates readily and has a relatively low boiling point.

4. Why water is not normally used in a liquid-in-glass thermometer
- It wets glass, making a clear meniscus difficult to read.
- It is colourless unless dyed.
- It does not expand uniformly over its full range; between 0 °C and 4 °C it contracts when warmed.
- Its useful liquid range is limited because it freezes near 0 °C and boils near 100 °C at standard atmospheric pressure.

5. Clinical thermometer
A clinical thermometer is designed to measure human body temperature. Traditional glass clinical thermometers have a narrow scale around normal body temperature (commonly about 35–42 °C). Read it at eye level and follow the maker's cleaning instructions. Do not sterilise a traditional clinical thermometer by putting it in boiling water: boiling water is far above its intended range and may damage or break it. Digital clinical thermometers have no mercury.

6. Evaporation
Evaporation is the change of a liquid into vapour from its surface. It can occur at temperatures below the boiling point. It produces cooling because the more energetic surface molecules escape. Evaporation is faster when:
- temperature is higher;
- the exposed surface area is larger;
- air moves faster across the surface (wind removes vapour);
- the surrounding air is less humid.

7. Boiling
Boiling is rapid vaporisation throughout a liquid when its vapour pressure equals the pressure acting on its surface. Bubbles form within the liquid. For pure water at standard atmospheric pressure, the boiling point is 100 °C. The boiling point changes with external pressure: higher pressure raises it and lower pressure lowers it. Wind is not the defining condition for boiling; it mainly affects evaporation from a surface.

8. Evaporation and boiling compared
Evaporation occurs only at the surface and can occur at many temperatures below the boiling point; it does not require bubbles throughout the liquid and causes cooling. Boiling occurs throughout the liquid at its boiling point for the prevailing pressure; bubbles form and the liquid temperature remains approximately constant while the pure liquid boils at constant pressure.

9. Fixed points and thermometer scales
The lower fixed point is the temperature of pure melting ice at standard atmospheric pressure: 0 °C, 32 °F and approximately 273 K. The upper fixed point is the temperature of steam above pure boiling water at standard pressure: 100 °C, 212 °F and approximately 373 K. The fundamental interval is 100 Celsius degrees, 180 Fahrenheit degrees or 100 kelvins.
For ordinary SS1 conversions use:
K ≈ °C + 273;   °C ≈ K − 273.
The more precise offset is 273.15.
For a Celsius scale:
θC/100 = (θF − 32)/180 = (T K − 273)/100.
For any uniform thermometer with lower fixed point L, upper fixed point U and reading R:
Celsius temperature = 100 × (R − L)/(U − L).

Worked example
A thermometer reads −20 at the ice point and 100 at the steam point. When it reads 70, the Celsius temperature is:
θC = 100 × (70 − (−20))/(100 − (−20)) = 100 × 90/120 = 75 °C.

10. Absolute zero
Absolute zero is 0 K, approximately −273.15 °C. It is the lower limit of the thermodynamic temperature scale. Do not describe it as a temperature at which all microscopic motion simply stops.

11. Source notation and correction notes
The source writes “resistant thermometer”; the correct term is resistance thermometer. The mercury freezing point is about −38.8 °C, not +39 °C. The source's question about wind, solar energy, liquid volume and container thickness “affecting boiling” is ambiguous: heat input affects the rate of heating, while external pressure determines the boiling point. A clearer assessment question is used in the practice set.

practice.question: Define a thermometer and a thermometric property.
practice.answer: A thermometer is an instrument for measuring temperature. A thermometric property is a measurable property that changes predictably with temperature.

practice.question: Name five types of thermometer and state the thermometric substance/property used by each.
practice.answer: Liquid-in-glass: mercury/alcohol volume or column length. Constant-volume gas: gas pressure. Thermocouple: thermoelectric e.m.f. Resistance thermometer: resistance of a wire. Bimetallic: differential expansion of two metals.

practice.question: State four differences between evaporation and boiling.
practice.answer: Evaporation occurs at the surface; boiling occurs throughout the liquid. Evaporation can occur below the boiling point at many temperatures; boiling occurs at the boiling point for the prevailing pressure. Evaporation does not produce bubbles throughout the liquid; boiling does. Evaporation causes cooling; during steady boiling at constant pressure, the liquid temperature remains approximately constant.

marking.criterion: Any temperature below boiling versus boiling point.
No bulk bubbles versus bubbles throughout.

practice.question: Give four reasons why water is not normally used as the liquid in a liquid-in-glass thermometer.
practice.answer: It wets glass; it is colourless; it expands anomalously/non-uniformly between 0 °C and 4 °C; and its useful liquid range is limited by freezing near 0 °C and boiling near 100 °C at standard pressure.

practice.question: State two advantages and two disadvantages of mercury or alcohol as a thermometric liquid.
practice.answer: Mercury: does not wet glass, is visible and expands fairly uniformly; disadvantages include toxicity, cost and freezing near −38.8 °C. Alcohol: inexpensive, expands more and has a very low freezing point; disadvantages include wetting glass, being colourless unless dyed, volatility and a lower boiling point.

marking.criterion: One correct advantage of either liquid.

practice.question: What is a clinical thermometer used for, and why should a traditional glass clinical thermometer not be sterilised in boiling water?
practice.answer: It measures human body temperature. Boiling water is far above its narrow operating range and may damage or break the thermometer.

marking.criterion: States that it measures human body temperature.
Notes its narrow range around body temperature.
Explains boiling water may damage/break it.

practice.question: Convert 7 °C to kelvin using the SS1 approximation.
A uniform thermometer reads −20 at the ice point and 100 at the steam point. What Celsius temperature corresponds to a reading of 70?
What is absolute zero? Give its value in kelvin and approximate Celsius.
practice.answer: Absolute zero is the lower limit of the thermodynamic temperature scale: 0 K, approximately −273.15 °C.

practice.question: Which thermometer is designed for measuring human body temperature? A. Resistance B. Clinical C. Thermoelectric D. Bimetallic.
practice.answer: B. Clinical thermometer.

practice.question: Give one important reason mercury can be used at temperatures below 0 °C in a thermometer.
practice.answer: Mercury has a low freezing point, about −38.8 °C.

practice.question: State two factors that increase the rate of evaporation.
practice.answer: Higher temperature, larger exposed surface area, faster air movement/wind, or lower humidity.

practice.question: A source question asks which of wind, solar energy, liquid volume or container thickness “affects boiling”. Explain why this wording is unclear and state what determines the boiling point.
practice.answer: Heat input affects how quickly a liquid is heated, while the boiling point is determined by the external pressure (and the liquid's composition/purity). Wind mainly affects evaporation, so the original options do not clearly identify the intended factor.

marking.criterion: Distinguishes heating rate from boiling point.
Identifies external pressure as determining the boiling point.

lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: Reading a micrometer screw gauge
objectives: Identify the main parts of a micrometer screw gauge and state what it measures.
Define pitch and calculate the least count from pitch and circular-scale divisions.
Find an observed reading by adding the main-scale reading to the circular-scale reading multiplied by the least count.
Identify zero error and calculate the corrected reading using the signed zero error.
Express a micrometer reading consistently in millimetres and centimetres.
lessons.body:
MICROMETER SCREW GAUGE: HOW TO READ IT

A micrometer screw gauge measures very small external dimensions, such as the diameter of a thin wire or the thickness of a sheet. The Week Two source names these uses and gives a reading increment of 0.01 mm, but it does not state a complete reading rule. This supplement supplies that rule. It is not a transcription of the source, and no value is taken from the uninspected Fig. 3.4.

1. Main parts
- Frame: supports the instrument.
- Anvil: the fixed measuring face.
- Spindle: the moving measuring face.
- Sleeve or barrel: carries the main (linear) scale and its reference line.
- Thimble: carries the circular scale and turns the screw.
- Ratchet stop: helps apply gentle, repeatable pressure.
- Lock: holds the spindle in position when a reading is being recorded.

2. Pitch and least count
The pitch is the distance the spindle advances during one complete turn of the thimble. The least count (LC) is the distance represented by one division on the circular scale:

LC = pitch ÷ number of circular-scale divisions.

For example, if the pitch is 0.5 mm and the circular scale has 50 equal divisions:

LC = 0.5 mm ÷ 50 = 0.01 mm.

Do not assume every instrument has the same pitch or number of divisions. Read the instrument's stated scale and calculate its least count.

3. Taking an observed reading
1. Check that the measuring faces are clean.
2. Close the anvil and spindle gently with the ratchet. Check whether the zero marks coincide; if not, determine the zero error.
3. Place the object between the faces and turn the ratchet until it grips gently. Do not force the thimble tight.
4. Read the last main-scale mark visible before the thimble edge. This is the main-scale reading (MSR).
5. Read the circular-scale division that coincides with the sleeve's reference line. Multiply that division by the least count to obtain the circular-scale reading.
6. Add the two parts:

Observed reading = MSR + (circular-scale division × LC).

4. Zero error and correction
Zero error is the reading shown when the measuring faces are fully closed. If the instrument reads zero when closed, its zero error is zero. If it does not, record the error with its sign.

Correct reading = observed reading − zero error.

Therefore:
- A positive zero error is subtracted from the observed reading.
- A negative zero error is also subtracted as a signed number, so its magnitude is added.

Always write the sign. Do not treat a negative zero error as positive.

5. Worked example (new example; not read from the source figure)
A micrometer has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 circular divisions. The main scale reading is 12.50 mm and the 34th circular division coincides with the reference line. There is no zero error.

LC = 0.5 ÷ 50 = 0.01 mm.
Circular-scale reading = 34 × 0.01 = 0.34 mm.
Observed reading = 12.50 + 0.34 = 12.84 mm.
Correct reading = 12.84 − 0 = 12.84 mm.
Since 10 mm = 1 cm, 12.84 mm = 1.284 cm.

The millimetre and centimetre readings agree.

6. Common errors to avoid
- Do not confuse pitch with least count.
- Do not multiply the main-scale reading by the least count.
- Do not read a circular division that does not meet the reference line.
- Do not forget zero correction.
- Do not over-tighten the object; use the ratchet.
- Keep units with every measurement.

Practice
Show the least-count calculation and the reading steps. The marks below are authored practice marks, not marks printed in the school source.

practice.question: A screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on its circular scale. The main-scale reading is 6.50 mm and the 32nd circular division coincides with the reference line. Find the least count and the observed reading. There is no zero error.
practice.answer: LC = 0.5/50 = 0.01 mm. Circular reading = 32 × 0.01 = 0.32 mm. Observed reading = 6.50 + 0.32 = 6.82 mm.

practice.question: A micrometer gives an observed reading of 8.27 mm. Its zero error is +0.03 mm. Find the corrected reading.
practice.answer: Corrected reading = observed reading − zero error = 8.27 − (+0.03) = 8.24 mm.

marking.criterion: States the correction rule: subtract the signed zero error

practice.question: The main-scale reading is 4.50 mm and the circular scale reading is 18 divisions. The least count is 0.01 mm and the zero error is −0.02 mm. Calculate the corrected reading.
practice.answer: Observed reading = 4.50 + (18 × 0.01) = 4.68 mm. Corrected reading = 4.68 − (−0.02) = 4.70 mm.

marking.criterion: Correctly adds the negative zero correction to obtain 4.70 mm

practice.question: Convert a corrected micrometer reading of 4.70 mm to centimetres.

lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: Thermal expansivity: linear, area, volume, liquids and anomalous expansion of water
objectives: Define linear, area and volume expansivity and state their SI units.
Use the equations for linear, area and volume expansion in calculations.
Explain the approximate relationships β ≈ 2α and γ ≈ 3α for small expansion of isotropic solids.
Distinguish real and apparent expansivity of a liquid and calculate container expansivity.
Explain the anomalous expansion of water between 0 °C and 4 °C and its importance.
lessons.body:
THERMAL EXPANSIVITY: LINEAR, AREA AND VOLUME

1. Meaning of thermal expansivity
Thermal expansion is the increase in a material's dimensions when its temperature rises. Thermal expansivity (coefficient of expansion) measures the fractional increase in a dimension per unit rise in temperature. The SI unit of each coefficient is kelvin⁻¹ (K⁻¹). A temperature rise of 1 °C has the same size as a rise of 1 K, so coefficients may also be expressed per °C.

Use ΔT = T₂ − T₁. A temperature difference is used in the equations; do not substitute an absolute Celsius or Kelvin reading for ΔT.

2. Linear expansivity (α)
Linear expansivity describes the fractional increase in length per unit original length for each unit temperature rise:
α = ΔL / (L₀ΔT)
Therefore:
ΔL = αL₀ΔT
L = L₀ + ΔL = L₀(1 + αΔT)
where L₀ is original length, L is final length and ΔL is the increase in length. α is measured in K⁻¹.

Worked example 1
A brass rod is 2.00 m long. Its linear expansivity is 18 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹. Find its final length after a temperature rise of 100 K.
ΔL = αL₀ΔT
= 18 × 10⁻⁶ × 2.00 × 100
= 0.0036 m.
Final length = 2.00 + 0.0036 = 2.0036 m.

3. Area (superficial) expansivity (β)
Area expansivity describes the fractional increase in surface area per unit original area per unit temperature rise:
β = ΔA / (A₀ΔT)
ΔA = βA₀ΔT
A = A₀(1 + βΔT)
For a uniform (isotropic) solid and a small temperature change, β ≈ 2α. This is because both length dimensions expand. The approximation ignores the very small product term (αΔT)².

Worked example 2
A metal plate has an original area of 0.50 m². Its area expansivity is 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹ and its temperature rises by 50 K.
ΔA = βA₀ΔT
= 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.50 × 50
= 0.00060 m².
Final area = 0.50060 m².

4. Volume (cubical) expansivity (γ)
Volume expansivity describes the fractional increase in volume per unit original volume per unit temperature rise:
γ = ΔV / (V₀ΔT)
ΔV = γV₀ΔT
V = V₀(1 + γΔT)
For a uniform isotropic solid and a small temperature change, γ ≈ 3α. Thus the approximate relationship for such solids is α : β : γ = 1 : 2 : 3. Do not apply this ratio blindly to every material or to liquids.

Worked example 3
A solid block has volume 1.50 × 10⁻³ m³. Its volume expansivity is 3.6 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹. Find the increase in volume for a temperature rise of 40 K.
ΔV = γV₀ΔT
= 3.6 × 10⁻⁵ × 1.50 × 10⁻³ × 40
= 2.16 × 10⁻⁶ m³.

5. Expansion of liquids: real and apparent
A liquid is normally heated in a container, and the container also expands. The liquid's actual increase in volume is called its real (or absolute) expansion. The increase observed relative to the expanding container is its apparent expansion.
For small temperature changes:
γᵣ = γₐ + γ꜀
where γᵣ is the real expansivity of the liquid, γₐ is its apparent expansivity, and γ꜀ is the cubical expansivity of the container.
Therefore:
γ꜀ = γᵣ − γₐ.
The apparent expansion is smaller than the real expansion when the container also expands. Use the same temperature interval and reference volume when comparing the coefficients.

Worked example 4
A liquid has real expansivity 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹ and apparent expansivity 2.8 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹ in a container. Find the container's cubical expansivity.
γ꜀ = γᵣ − γₐ
= (3.0 − 2.8) × 10⁻⁴
= 0.2 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹.

6. Anomalous expansion of water
Most liquids expand when heated and contract when cooled. Water behaves unusually between 0 °C and 4 °C:
- When water is heated from 0 °C to 4 °C, it contracts and its density increases.
- At about 4 °C, water has its maximum density (approximately 1,000 kg m⁻³ at standard atmospheric pressure).
- When water is heated above 4 °C, it expands normally.
- When water cools from 4 °C towards 0 °C, it expands. On freezing, it expands further, so ice is less dense than liquid water and floats.
This behaviour helps lakes and ponds freeze from the surface rather than becoming solid ice from the bottom upward.

7. How to solve expansivity questions
1. Write down the quantity being asked for: ΔL, ΔA, ΔV, a coefficient or a final dimension.
2. Record the original dimension and the temperature change ΔT.
3. Choose the matching equation: α for length, β for area, γ for volume.
4. Convert all dimensions to consistent units before substituting.
5. Keep the coefficient in K⁻¹ and the temperature change in K or °C.
6. Give the final answer with the correct unit and sensible significant figures.

COMMON ERRORS TO AVOID
- Using the final temperature instead of the temperature change.
- Forgetting to add the increase to the original length/area/volume when the question asks for the final dimension.
- Confusing α, β and γ or omitting K⁻¹.
- Treating β = 2α and γ = 3α as exact for large expansions or all materials.
- Saying water expands normally throughout 0–4 °C; in this interval it contracts when heated.
- Confusing real expansion of a liquid with apparent expansion measured in an expanding vessel.

SUMMARY
α = ΔL/(L₀ΔT); β = ΔA/(A₀ΔT); γ = ΔV/(V₀ΔT).
For small expansions of isotropic solids: β ≈ 2α and γ ≈ 3α.
For a liquid in an expanding container: γᵣ = γₐ + γ꜀.
Water has maximum density near 4 °C and expands anomalously between 0 °C and 4 °C.

practice.question: Define linear expansivity and state its SI unit.
practice.answer: Linear expansivity is the fractional increase in length per unit original length per unit temperature rise. Its SI unit is K⁻¹.

marking.criterion: Gives the fractional increase in length per unit original length per degree.

practice.question: Write the equations for change in length and final length of a uniformly heated rod.
practice.answer: ΔL = αL₀ΔT and L = L₀(1 + αΔT).

practice.question: A brass rod is 2.00 m long, α = 18 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ and its temperature rises by 100 K. Find its final length.
Define area expansivity and state its approximate relationship with linear expansivity for an isotropic solid.
practice.answer: Area expansivity is the fractional increase in area per unit original area per unit temperature rise. For small expansion, β ≈ 2α.

practice.question: A plate has area 0.50 m², β = 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹ and is heated by 50 K. Calculate its increase in area.
State the approximate relationship between the volume and linear expansivities of an isotropic solid for small expansion.
practice.answer: γ ≈ 3α.

practice.question: A solid has V₀ = 1.50 × 10⁻³ m³, γ = 3.6 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹ and ΔT = 40 K. Find the increase in volume.
Distinguish between real and apparent expansion of a liquid.
practice.answer: Real expansion is the actual increase in the liquid's volume. Apparent expansion is the increase observed relative to the container, which also expands when heated.

marking.criterion: Correctly defines apparent expansion and mentions container expansion.

practice.question: A liquid has real expansivity 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹ and apparent expansivity 2.8 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹. Calculate the container's cubical expansivity.

marking.criterion: Uses γᵣ = γₐ + γ꜀ or rearranges correctly.

practice.question: Explain the anomalous expansion of water between 0 °C and 4 °C.
practice.answer: When water is heated from 0 °C to 4 °C it contracts and becomes denser. At about 4 °C it has maximum density. Above 4 °C it expands normally.

marking.criterion: States that water contracts when heated from 0 °C to 4 °C.
States that density is maximum at about 4 °C.
States that above 4 °C it expands normally.

practice.question: At approximately what temperature does pure water have its maximum density at normal atmospheric pressure?
practice.answer: Approximately 4 °C.

practice.question: For a small temperature rise in an isotropic solid, what is the approximate ratio α : β : γ?
When water is heated from 1 °C to 3 °C, what happens to its volume? (A) It increases (B) It decreases (C) It remains constant (D) It becomes zero.
practice.answer: B. It decreases because water contracts as it is heated within the 0–4 °C interval.

practice.question: Why does ice float on liquid water, and why is this important for ponds?
practice.answer: Water expands on freezing, making ice less dense than liquid water, so it floats. A surface layer of ice can insulate the water below, allowing aquatic life to survive in colder conditions.

marking.criterion: States that water expands on freezing.
Connects expansion with lower density and floating.
Explains surface freezing/insulation of water below.

practice.question: A metal is 15.01 m long. After its temperature rises by 60 K, its length is 15.05 m. Calculate its linear expansivity.

marking.criterion: Uses α = ΔL/(L₀ΔT) and substitutes correctly.

practice.question: The volume of 10 cm³ of mercury increases by 0.182 cm³ when its temperature rises by 100 K. Calculate its cubical expansivity.
A metal bar 50 cm long is heated from 15 °C to 85 °C and expands by 0.088 cm. Find its linear expansivity.

marking.criterion: Uses α = ΔL/(L₀ΔT) and substitutes correctly.

practice.question: Show that the area expansivity of an isotropic solid is approximately twice its linear expansivity for small expansion.
practice.answer: For a rectangular plate, L₂ = L₁(1 + αΔT) and b₂ = b₁(1 + αΔT). Therefore A₂ = A₁(1 + αΔT)² ≈ A₁(1 + 2αΔT), ignoring the small (αΔT)² term. Comparing with A₂ = A₁(1 + βΔT), β ≈ 2α.

marking.criterion: Writes the expanded length and breadth relations.
Neglects the small squared term for small expansion.

practice.question: A liquid has real expansivity 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ and apparent expansivity 1.8 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹. Find the cubical expansivity of its container.
The linear expansivity of metal P is twice that of metal Q. They are heated through the same temperature rise and have equal increases in length. Find the ratio of their original lengths Lₚ : Lq.
practice.answer: αₚLₚΔT = αqLqΔT. Since αₚ = 2αq, 2αqLₚ = αqLq, so Lₚ/Lq = 1/2. Ratio = 1 : 2.

lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: Heat transfer: conduction, convection, radiation, sea breeze and vacuum flask
objectives: Define conduction, convection and radiation and distinguish the three methods.
Explain conduction in solids, including the role of mobile electrons in metals.
Explain convection currents in liquids and gases.
Explain the formation of sea breeze and land breeze using convection.
Describe thermal radiation and the behaviour of dull black and shiny surfaces.
Explain how the parts of a vacuum flask reduce conduction, convection and radiation.
lessons.body:
HEAT TRANSFER: CONDUCTION, CONVECTION AND RADIATION

1. What is heat transfer?
Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Heat flows spontaneously from a region at higher temperature to one at lower temperature. The three main methods are conduction, convection and radiation. More than one method may operate at the same time.

2. Conduction
Conduction is the transfer of thermal energy through a material without bulk movement of the material from one place to another.
- In solids, neighbouring particles pass energy through vibrations and interactions.
- In metals, mobile electrons also carry energy quickly, which is why most metals are good thermal conductors.
- Wood, plastic, rubber, trapped air and many other non-metals are relatively poor conductors (insulators).

Example: If one end of a metal rod is heated, energy is passed from the hot region towards the cooler end. The rod itself does not flow from one end to the other.

Uses and applications
- Cooking pots and kettles are commonly made from metals because metals conduct heat to the food or water.
- Handles may be made from wood or heat-resistant plastic because these are poor conductors and reduce burns.
- Woollen clothing, foam and trapped air reduce heat loss because they are poor conductors.
- Thick walls and roof insulation slow heat transfer into or out of buildings.

3. Convection
Convection is heat transfer in a fluid (a liquid or gas) by the bulk movement of the fluid.
When part of a fluid is heated, it usually expands and becomes less dense than the cooler fluid around it. The warmer, less dense fluid rises while cooler, denser fluid moves in to replace it. This circulation forms a convection current. Convection cannot occur in a solid in the ordinary fluid-flow sense because the particles in a solid do not flow from place to place.

Example: Water heated at the bottom of a pot becomes warmer and less dense, rises, and is replaced by cooler water. The circulating water distributes thermal energy.

Sea breeze (daytime)
1. During the day, land usually heats up faster than the sea.
2. Air above the warmer land is heated, expands, becomes less dense and rises.
3. Cooler, denser air above the sea moves towards the land to replace the rising air.
4. This movement of cooler air from sea to land is called a sea breeze.
The return flow occurs higher in the atmosphere. The explanation depends on unequal heating and convection, not on the sea producing cold air by itself.

Land breeze (night-time)
At night, land usually cools faster than the sea. Air above the relatively warmer sea rises, and cooler air from the land moves towards the sea. This is called a land breeze.

4. Radiation
Radiation is the transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves. Thermal radiation is mainly infrared for bodies at ordinary temperatures. Radiation does not require a material medium, so energy from the Sun can travel through the vacuum of space to Earth.
- Dull, dark surfaces are generally good absorbers and good emitters of thermal radiation.
- Shiny, polished surfaces are generally poor absorbers and poor emitters; they reflect more radiation.
- A hot object can transfer energy by radiation even when the air between it and another object is not moving.

Examples and applications
- Heat from a fire can reach a person across a room mainly by radiation.
- Solar heaters use radiation from the Sun.
- A light-coloured or reflective roof can reduce absorption of solar radiation.
- A dark, dull cooking surface absorbs radiant energy effectively.

5. Comparing the three methods
Conduction: requires matter; energy passes through the material without bulk flow.
Convection: requires a moving fluid; energy is carried by the fluid's bulk movement.
Radiation: does not require matter; energy travels as electromagnetic waves.
A hot pot may transfer energy to its metal body by conduction, circulate heat through water by convection, and emit infrared radiation to its surroundings.

6. The vacuum flask (thermos flask)
A vacuum flask reduces the rate at which thermal energy enters or leaves its contents. It does not stop heat transfer perfectly.
- Double walls with a vacuum between them: the vacuum greatly reduces conduction and prevents convection across the gap because there are very few particles to transfer energy.
- Silvered or shiny facing surfaces: reflect thermal radiation and reduce transfer by radiation.
- Insulating stopper (cork or suitable plastic): reduces conduction through the opening and limits air movement and evaporation.
- Insulating supports at the base and narrow contact points: reduce conduction through the supports.
- A tight lid: reduces air exchange and evaporation.
A flask keeps hot liquid hot for longer or cold liquid cold for longer by slowing all three methods of heat transfer.

7. How to identify the method in a question
- Energy passes along a metal rod: conduction.
- Warm water or air rises and cooler fluid replaces it: convection.
- Energy travels from the Sun or a fire across a vacuum/space: radiation.
- A vacuum between flask walls: reduces conduction and convection.
- Silvered flask surfaces: reduce radiation.

COMMON ERRORS
- Conduction is not the same as convection: conduction does not require bulk flow of the material.
- Convection occurs in fluids, not through a rigid solid.
- Radiation does not need air or another medium.
- A vacuum flask's vacuum does not prevent radiation; the reflective surfaces reduce radiation.
- A thermos flask slows heat transfer; it does not make heat transfer impossible.

SUMMARY
Conduction transfers energy through matter without bulk movement. Convection transfers energy by bulk movement of a fluid. Radiation transfers energy by electromagnetic waves and needs no medium. A vacuum flask reduces conduction, convection and radiation using a vacuum gap, reflective surfaces, insulation and a tight stopper.

practice.question: Define conduction of heat.
practice.answer: Conduction is the transfer of thermal energy through a material without bulk movement of the material from place to place.

marking.criterion: States that it is transfer of thermal energy through a material.
States that there is no bulk movement of the material.

practice.question: Why are metals generally good conductors of heat?
practice.answer: Energy is transferred by interactions/vibrations between particles, and mobile electrons in metals also carry thermal energy rapidly through the metal.

practice.question: Define convection.
practice.answer: Convection is the transfer of thermal energy in a liquid or gas by the bulk movement of the fluid.

marking.criterion: Identifies transfer of thermal energy in a fluid.
States that bulk fluid movement carries the energy.

practice.question: Explain how a convection current is formed in water heated from below.
practice.answer: The water near the heat source warms, expands and becomes less dense, so it rises. Cooler, denser water moves down to replace it. The circulation continues and transfers energy.

marking.criterion: Cooler, denser water replaces it and a circulation forms.

practice.question: Explain how a sea breeze forms during the day.
practice.answer: Land heats faster than the sea. Air above the land warms, expands, becomes less dense and rises. Cooler, denser air from above the sea moves towards the land to replace it; this is the sea breeze.

marking.criterion: States that land heats faster than sea in daytime.
Explains that warm air over land rises.
States that cooler, denser sea air moves towards land.
Identifies this flow as a sea breeze.

practice.question: What is a land breeze, and when does it commonly occur?
practice.answer: A land breeze is the movement of cooler air from land towards the sea, commonly at night when land cools faster than the sea and warmer air above the sea rises.

marking.criterion: States direction from land to sea.
States that it commonly occurs at night.
Explains the temperature difference/rising warm air over sea.

practice.question: Define thermal radiation.
practice.answer: Thermal radiation is the transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves, mainly infrared at ordinary temperatures.

marking.criterion: States that energy is transferred by electromagnetic waves.
Identifies infrared as the main thermal radiation at ordinary temperatures.

practice.question: Why can heat from the Sun reach the Earth even though space is almost a vacuum?
practice.answer: Radiation is carried by electromagnetic waves and does not require a material medium.

marking.criterion: States that no material medium is required.

practice.question: Compare dull black and shiny polished surfaces as absorbers and emitters of thermal radiation.
practice.answer: Dull black surfaces are generally good absorbers and good emitters. Shiny polished surfaces are generally poor absorbers and poor emitters and reflect more radiation.

marking.criterion: Dull black surfaces are good absorbers.
Dull black surfaces are good emitters.
Shiny surfaces are poor absorbers/emitters and reflect more.

practice.question: What two methods of heat transfer are greatly reduced by the vacuum between the walls of a thermos flask?
practice.answer: Conduction and convection.

practice.question: What is the function of the silvered surfaces in a vacuum flask?
practice.answer: They reflect thermal radiation and reduce heat transfer by radiation.

marking.criterion: States that the surfaces reflect thermal radiation.
Connects this with reduced radiative heat transfer.

practice.question: Give two functions of the stopper and insulating supports of a thermos flask.
practice.answer: The stopper reduces conduction through the opening and limits air movement/evaporation. Insulating supports reduce conduction through the points where the inner vessel is held.

practice.question: Match each situation with the main method of heat transfer: (a) a metal spoon gets hot in soup; (b) warm air rises above a heater; (c) energy from the Sun reaches Earth.
practice.answer: (a) Conduction; (b) convection; (c) radiation.

practice.question: Name the main method of heat transfer in each part: (a) heat travels through the metal body of a pot; (b) water circulates inside the pot; (c) the hot pot emits energy to the room.
practice.answer: (a) Conduction; (b) convection; (c) radiation.

practice.question: A vacuum flask has a vacuum between its walls. Which method is NOT prevented by the vacuum? (A) conduction (B) convection (C) radiation (D) both conduction and convection.
practice.answer: C. Radiation. Reflective surfaces are used to reduce radiation.

practice.question: Why are saucepan handles often made from wood or heat-resistant plastic rather than metal?
practice.answer: Wood and suitable plastics are poor conductors of heat, so less thermal energy is conducted to the hand and the risk of burns is reduced.

marking.criterion: Connects this with reduced heat transfer/burn risk.

lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: Electric charges: production, types, distribution and storage
objectives: Explain static electricity and distinguish positive and negative charge.
Explain charging by friction in terms of electron transfer and conservation of charge.
State and apply the fundamental law of electrostatics.
Describe charging by friction, contact and induction.
Explain charge distribution on a conductor and concentration at sharp points.
Describe capacitors and electrophorus as devices for storing or transferring charge.
lessons.body:
ELECTRIC CHARGES: PRODUCTION, TYPES, DISTRIBUTION AND STORAGE

1. Static electricity
Electric charge is a property of matter that causes electrical attraction and repulsion. Static electricity is charge that has built up on an object rather than flowing continuously through a circuit.
There are two kinds of electric charge: positive (+) and negative (−). An ordinary atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons and is electrically neutral. Protons carry positive charge; electrons carry negative charge. In ordinary charging by rubbing, electrons move from one material to another. Protons do not move from one solid object to another.

2. How charging by friction occurs
When two different materials are rubbed together, electrons may transfer from one surface to the other:
- The object that gains electrons becomes negatively charged.
- The object that loses electrons becomes positively charged.
- The total charge of the two-object system is conserved: charge is transferred, not created from nothing.
Examples:
- An ebonite/plastic rod rubbed with fur commonly gains electrons and becomes negative; the fur becomes positive.
- A glass rod rubbed with silk commonly loses electrons and becomes positive; the silk becomes negative.
The exact result depends on the materials and their condition. Rubbing is a way of bringing the surfaces into close contact; it is not friction magically creating charge.

3. The fundamental law of electrostatics
- Like charges repel: positive repels positive, and negative repels negative.
- Unlike charges attract: positive attracts negative.
- A charged object can also attract a neutral light object. The charged object causes charges in the neutral object to redistribute slightly (polarisation), producing a net attraction. Therefore, attraction alone does not prove that an object has the opposite charge.

4. Ways of charging
A. Charging by friction: rubbing two materials transfers electrons between them.
B. Charging by contact (conduction): a charged object touches a conductor and some charge is transferred. The conductor may acquire the same sign as the charging object.
C. Charging by induction: a charged object is brought near a conductor without touching it. Charges in the conductor separate. With suitable earthing and removal steps, the conductor can be left with a net charge, usually opposite in sign to the inducing object. Induction does not require direct contact.

5. Distribution of charge on a conductor
On a conductor, excess charge can move. In electrostatic equilibrium, excess charge is found on the outer surface. The distribution is not always uniform:
- Charge is more concentrated at sharp points and regions of small radius of curvature.
- The electric field is strongest near these sharp regions.
- This is the principle behind the action of lightning conductors and points used to discharge charge from objects.
A smooth spherical conductor has a more uniform surface distribution than a conductor with sharp projections.

6. Storage of electric charge
A capacitor stores electric charge and energy in the electric field between two conductors separated by an insulating material called a dielectric.
- The two conductors are called plates or electrodes.
- When connected to a source, one plate gains negative charge and the other becomes positively charged.
- The dielectric prevents direct contact between the plates and helps maintain the electric field.
- A capacitor is used in electronic circuits, power supplies, camera flashes and many timing/control circuits.
Capacitance is the charge stored per unit potential difference:
C = Q/V
where C is capacitance in farads (F), Q is charge in coulombs (C) and V is potential difference in volts (V).
An electrophorus is another electrostatic device. It uses induction to transfer charge to a metal plate; it is not the same thing as a capacitor used for long-term energy storage.

7. Simple observations
A rubbed plastic pen may attract small pieces of paper. The pen is charged and polarises the neutral paper, producing attraction.
A charged electroscope can indicate the presence of charge by the divergence of its leaves. The gold-leaf electroscope is studied in the next week.

COMMON ERRORS
- A neutral object is not an object with no charges; it has equal positive and negative charges.
- Rubbing transfers electrons; it does not create charge.
- Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
- A neutral object can be attracted to a charged object through polarisation.
- A capacitor stores charge and electrical energy; an electrophorus is an electrostatic induction device.
- Charge concentration is greatest near sharp points, not necessarily at the centre of a conductor.

SUMMARY
Positive and negative are the two kinds of charge. Rubbing, contact and induction can charge objects. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Excess charge on a conductor resides on its outer surface and concentrates near sharp points. A capacitor stores charge and energy in an electric field.

practice.question: What is static electricity?
practice.answer: Static electricity is electric charge that has built up on an object and is not flowing continuously through a circuit.

marking.criterion: Identifies it as an accumulation/build-up of electric charge.
Distinguishes it from continuous current flow.

practice.question: Name the two types of electric charge.
practice.answer: Positive charge and negative charge.

practice.question: A plastic rod is rubbed with fur and becomes negatively charged. Explain the transfer of charge and state the sign of the fur.
practice.answer: Electrons transfer from the fur to the plastic rod. The rod gains electrons and becomes negative; the fur loses electrons and becomes positive.

marking.criterion: States that electrons move from fur to rod.
Explains that the rod gains electrons and becomes negative.
States that the fur becomes positive.

practice.question: State the fundamental law of electrostatics.
practice.answer: Like charges repel each other, while unlike charges attract each other.

practice.question: Why can a charged plastic pen attract small pieces of neutral paper?
practice.answer: The charged pen causes charges in each neutral paper piece to redistribute (polarise). The nearer side becomes effectively oppositely charged, producing a net attraction.

marking.criterion: Mentions redistribution/polarisation of charge in the paper.

practice.question: Name three methods of charging an object and briefly describe each.
practice.answer: Friction: rubbing transfers electrons. Contact/conduction: a charged object touches a conductor and transfers charge. Induction: a charged object brought near a conductor causes charge separation; with earthing and removal it can leave a net charge without contact.

practice.question: Explain how a conductor can be charged by induction.
practice.answer: Bring a charged body near the conductor without touching it so charges separate. Earth the conductor while the charged body is still near, remove the earth, then remove the charged body. The conductor is left with a net charge, usually opposite to the inducing body.

marking.criterion: Brings charged body near without contact and causes charge separation.
Uses earthing while the inducing body remains near.
Removes earth before the inducing body and states the conductor is left charged.

practice.question: Where is excess charge found on a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium?
practice.answer: On the outer surface of the conductor.

practice.question: Why is charge more concentrated near a sharp point on a conductor?
practice.answer: A sharp point has a small radius of curvature. Surface charge density and the electric field are greater there than on a gently curved region.

marking.criterion: Identifies the sharp point/small radius of curvature.
Connects it with greater surface charge density/stronger electric field.

practice.question: Explain the electrostatic principle used by a pointed lightning conductor.
practice.answer: Charge is concentrated at sharp points, producing a strong electric field that can encourage charge leakage/corona discharge. A properly earthed lightning protection system also provides a low-resistance path for lightning current safely to ground.

marking.criterion: Mentions charge concentration/strong field at the point.
Mentions charge leakage/discharge or the protective action of the point.
States that the conductor is earthed to carry current to ground.

practice.question: What is a capacitor and what does it store?
practice.answer: A capacitor is a device made of two conductors separated by an insulating dielectric. It stores electric charge and energy in the electric field between its plates.

marking.criterion: States that it stores charge and electrical energy.

practice.question: A capacitor stores 6 μC of charge at a potential difference of 12 V. Calculate its capacitance.
What is an electrophorus used for?
practice.answer: An electrophorus is an electrostatic device that uses induction to transfer charge to a metal plate.

marking.criterion: Identifies it as an electrostatic device.
States that it uses induction to transfer charge.

practice.question: Explain why charging by rubbing does not violate conservation of charge.
practice.answer: Rubbing transfers electrons from one material to another. One object gains the electrons lost by the other, so the total charge of the two-object system remains unchanged.

marking.criterion: States that electrons are transferred rather than created.
States that total charge is conserved.

practice.question: An ebonite rod rubbed with fur becomes (A) positive (B) negative (C) neutral (D) magnetic.
practice.answer: B. Negative.

practice.question: Like electric charges (A) attract (B) repel (C) evaporate (D) disappear.
practice.answer: B. Repel.

practice.question: Excess charge on a conductor is most concentrated near a surface that is (A) flat (B) sharply curved (C) perfectly insulated (D) buried inside the conductor.
practice.answer: B. Sharply curved.

practice.question: A rubbed biro attracts a small piece of paper mainly because (A) the pen is magnetised (B) the paper becomes a magnet (C) the charged pen polarises the neutral paper (D) gravity is removed.
practice.answer: C. The charged pen polarises the neutral paper.

lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: Gold-leaf electroscope: structure, uses, charge testing and lightning protection
objectives: Define an electroscope and identify its main parts and functions.
Explain how leaf divergence indicates the presence of charge.
Use a charged electroscope to test whether a material conducts and to compare the sign of an unknown charge.
Explain lightning and the protective function of an earthed lightning conductor.
Describe safe practice around thunderstorms and lightning protection systems.
lessons.body:
GOLD-LEAF ELECTROSCOPE: STRUCTURE, USES AND LIGHTNING PROTECTION

1. What is an electroscope?
An electroscope is an instrument used to detect the presence of electric charge. A gold-leaf electroscope is sensitive because its thin gold leaf is very light and moves when electric charge is redistributed.

2. Main parts and their functions
- Metal cap or disc: the part to which a charged object is brought or touched.
- Metal rod: conducts charge between the cap and the leaf.
- Gold leaf: the thin moving part; it diverges from the metal stem when like charges are present on both.
- Metal case: protects the leaf from draughts and physical damage.
- Earthed metal case: screens the leaf from many external electric-field effects and helps the instrument give a steadier reading.
- Insulating stopper: supports the rod while preventing charge from leaking to the case.

3. How the electroscope detects charge
When a charged object touches the cap, charge is transferred through the rod to the leaf and stem. The leaf and stem acquire like charges and repel, so the leaf diverges.
A charged object can also be brought near the cap without touching it. Charge separation occurs in the electroscope by induction and the leaf may diverge. The response shows that an electric influence is present; it does not by itself identify the sign of an unknown charge.

4. Testing whether an object is a conductor or an insulator
Charge the electroscope and touch the cap with the material being tested, while keeping the setup dry and clean.
- If charge flows away through the material and the leaf collapses quickly, the material is a good conductor (provided the other end offers a path for charge to escape).
- If the leaf remains diverged and charge does not readily escape, the material is a poor conductor or insulator.
A fair test must control the contact, earthing and moisture. A dry material may behave differently when damp.

5. Testing the sign of an unknown charge
First charge the electroscope with a known sign, for example negative, so its leaf is diverged. Bring the unknown charged object near the cap without touching it:
- If the divergence increases, the unknown charge has the same sign as the electroscope.
- If the divergence decreases, the unknown charge has the opposite sign.
The electroscope must already have a known charge for this comparison. A neutral electroscope cannot reliably tell the sign of an unknown charge by this simple test alone.

6. Lightning and lightning conductors
Lightning is a large electrical discharge between charged regions, such as within clouds or between a cloud and the ground. It can cause fire, injury and structural damage.
A lightning conductor (lightning rod) is a metal rod installed at a high point of a building and connected to the ground by a thick, low-resistance conductor. It provides a controlled path for lightning current to reach Earth rather than passing through the building.
- The rod is fixed securely at a suitable high point.
- A continuous, low-resistance metal down-conductor connects it to an effective earth electrode.
- The earthing system must be installed and maintained correctly.
A lightning conductor does not stop thunderstorms or guarantee that lightning will never strike. It reduces the risk of damage by providing a safer route for the discharge. Installation should follow applicable electrical and building-safety standards.

7. Safety and good practice
Never try to test lightning protection by creating a spark or using a high-voltage source. Do not touch an exposed lightning conductor during a storm. In a thunderstorm, move indoors or into a fully enclosed vehicle and stay away from open fields, isolated trees, metal fences and water.

COMMON ERRORS
- The leaf diverges because like charges repel; it does not move because it is attracted to the cap.
- The case is earthed to shield the leaf and reduce external interference, not to charge the leaf.
- To compare an unknown sign, first give the electroscope a known charge.
- Greater divergence means same sign only when a known charged electroscope is used.
- A lightning rod provides a safe path to Earth; it does not prevent lightning from occurring.

SUMMARY
A gold-leaf electroscope detects charge by leaf divergence. It can compare charge signs when it is first charged with a known sign, and it can help test conduction. A properly installed and earthed lightning conductor provides a safer path for lightning current to reach Earth.

practice.question: What is a gold-leaf electroscope used for?
practice.answer: It is used to detect the presence of electric charge.

marking.criterion: States that it detects electric charge.

practice.question: Name four main parts of a gold-leaf electroscope and state one function of each.
practice.answer: Metal cap receives or is approached by charge; metal rod conducts charge; gold leaf is the sensitive moving part; metal case protects and screens the leaf; insulating stopper supports the rod and prevents leakage. Any four.

practice.question: Why does the gold leaf diverge when charge reaches the electroscope?
practice.answer: The leaf and stem acquire like charges and repel each other, causing the thin leaf to move away from the stem.

marking.criterion: States that leaf and stem acquire like charges.

practice.question: Why is the metal case of a gold-leaf electroscope earthed?
practice.answer: It screens the leaf from external electric-field interference and helps protect the sensitive leaf, giving steadier readings.

marking.criterion: Mentions screening from external electric fields/interference.

practice.question: Describe how a gold-leaf electroscope detects a charged object.
practice.answer: Bring the object near the cap or touch it to the cap. Charge redistribution or transfer makes the leaf and stem acquire like charges; they repel and the leaf diverges.

marking.criterion: Brings the object near or into contact with the cap.

practice.question: How can an electroscope be used to test whether a material is a good conductor or an insulator?
practice.answer: Charge the electroscope and touch its cap with the material, providing a path for charge to escape. A conductor allows charge to flow away and the leaf collapses; an insulator does not allow charge to flow readily, so the leaf remains diverged.

marking.criterion: Describes charging the electroscope and touching the cap with the test material.
States that a conductor allows charge to escape and the leaf collapses.
States that an insulator retains charge and the leaf remains diverged.

practice.question: Describe the procedure for determining the sign of an unknown charge with a gold-leaf electroscope.
practice.answer: First charge the electroscope with a known sign and allow the leaf to diverge. Bring the unknown charged body near the cap without touching it. Increased divergence indicates the same sign; decreased divergence indicates the opposite sign.

marking.criterion: Charges the electroscope with a known sign.
Brings unknown body near without touching.

practice.question: A negatively charged electroscope has a diverged leaf. An unknown negatively charged rod is brought near its cap. What happens to the divergence and why?
practice.answer: The divergence increases because the rod and electroscope have the same (negative) sign; the rod's field drives more like charge towards the leaf, increasing repulsion.

marking.criterion: Explains that the charges have the same sign and repel.

practice.question: What is lightning?
practice.answer: Lightning is a large electrical discharge between charged regions, for example within clouds or between a cloud and the ground.

marking.criterion: Identifies it as an electrical discharge.
Gives a valid example of charged regions.

practice.question: Explain the purpose of a lightning conductor on a building.
practice.answer: It provides a low-resistance path for lightning current to travel safely to Earth, reducing the chance that the current will pass through and damage the building.

marking.criterion: States that it is connected to Earth/ground.
States that it provides a low-resistance path for the discharge.
Explains that it reduces building damage/risk.

practice.question: Does a lightning conductor prevent lightning from occurring? Explain.
practice.answer: No. It does not stop storms or lightning. It reduces damage by providing a safer path for lightning current to reach Earth.

marking.criterion: Explains the safer path to Earth.

practice.question: A capacitor is a device that (A) produces charge from nothing (B) stores electric charge and energy (C) detects only magnetic fields (D) measures mass.
practice.answer: B. It stores electric charge and energy.

practice.question: Why is the casing of a gold-leaf electroscope earthed? (A) to make the leaf positive (B) to screen the leaf from outside interference (C) to store charge (D) to attract lightning.
practice.answer: B. To screen the leaf from outside interference.

practice.question: A known negative charge is brought near a negatively charged electroscope. The leaf divergence (A) increases (B) decreases (C) disappears immediately (D) remains zero.
practice.answer: A. It increases because the charges have the same sign.

practice.question: Which instrument detects electric charge? (A) electrophorus (B) capacitor (C) gold-leaf electroscope (D) inductor.
practice.answer: C. Gold-leaf electroscope.

practice.question: State one important safety feature of a properly installed lightning-protection system.
practice.answer: A continuous, low-resistance down-conductor connected to an effective earth electrode provides a path for lightning current to reach ground.

marking.criterion: Mentions connection to an effective earth electrode.
